key_points.point_text: Central thesis: Can't Stop is a masterclass in practical game design, where imperfect mathematical balance is acceptable and rules are used to compensate for it.
key_points.evidence_quote: perfect balance isn't necessary, as the game is engaging despite (or because of) favoring middle columns
key_points.reasoning: Summary L002 and conclusion L088 both capture the thesis that near-balance is acceptable and rules compensate. The forced-move rule as compensating mechanism is stated at L036/L077.

key_points.point_text: Game rules: roll four dice, pair them to move markers on columns 2 through 12, need three completed columns to win; column lengths are 3,5,7,9,11,13,11,9,7,5,3.
key_points.evidence_quote: Column lengths run 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 11, 9, 7, 5, and 3 steps for columns 2 through 12.
key_points.reasoning: L003 states roll four dice, pair into sums, columns 2-12, three completed to win. L005 gives the full length sequence exactly.

key_points.point_text: Forced-move rule: if a chosen pairing creates any valid move you must take all legal moves from that pairing, even onto unwanted columns; you cannot cherry-pick.
key_points.evidence_quote: The forced-move rule requires taking all legal moves from a chosen pairing, even unwanted ones.
key_points.reasoning: L006 states the rule with the 'even unwanted ones' qualifier; L007 gives the {6,7,8} 2+7 example. Meaning intact.

key_points.point_text: Two-dice baseline: sum 7 is most likely at 16.67%, exactly 6 times more likely than sum 2 at 2.78%.
key_points.evidence_quote: With two dice, sum 7 is most likely at 16.67% and exactly 6× more likely than sum 2 at 2.78%.
key_points.reasoning: L011 carries both exact percentages and the 6x ratio with no qualifier loss.

key_points.point_text: With four dice the distribution flattens: P(can make 7) = 64.4% and P(can make 2) = 13.2%, only a 4.88x ratio versus 6x with two dice.
key_points.evidence_quote: P(7) = 64.4% versus P(2) = 13.2%, only a 4.88× difference
key_points.reasoning: L010 states 64.4% and 13.2%; L022 restates the 4.88x ratio in conclusion. The contrast with 6x is available via L011/L021.

key_points.point_text: Expected rolls to complete a column = length / probability; column 2 needs about 22.73 rolls while column 7 needs about 20.18, so 7 is slightly faster despite being 4x longer.
key_points.evidence_quote: column 2 needs 3/0.132 = 22.73 rolls; column 7 needs 13/0.644 = 20.18 ... Column 7 is slightly faster than column 2 even though it is 4× longer.
key_points.reasoning: L024 gives formula and both numbers; L025 preserves the surprising faster-despite-longer conclusion.

key_points.point_text: Column combinations matter: {6,7,8} succeeds 92.0% of the time versus 43.8% for {2,3,12}; all 165 three-column combinations were analyzed, with 37 rated excellent (>=85% success) and a median success of 79.6%.
key_points.evidence_quote: {6,7,8} succeeds on 1193/1296 rolls; {2,3,12} on only 568/1296 ... Across all 165 combinations, 37 are excellent at ≥85% success, the median is 79.6%
key_points.reasoning: L029 gives the 92.0%/43.8% contrast; L031 gives 165 combinations, 37 at >=85%, median 79.6%. All numbers and qualifiers intact.

key_points.point_text: "Clean" moves are rare: even the best combination {6,7,8} yields only 39.8% clean rolls, and {2,3,12} only 2.3%, so the forced-move rule contaminates good combinations.
key_points.evidence_quote: even {6,7,8} is clean only 39.8% of the time ... only 2.3% of {2,3,12} rolls are clean
key_points.reasoning: L034 gives 39.8% clean and the clean definition; L035 gives 2.3% and states forced moves contaminate good combinations.

key_points.point_text: Stopping heuristic: keep rolling if (P_success x Q) > (P_bust x U), where Q is expected markers advanced and U is unsaved progress; example on {6,7,8} says roll (1.32 > 0.4) and on {2,3,12} says stop (1.12 > 0.46).
key_points.evidence_quote: keep rolling if P(success) × Q exceeds P(bust) × U ... 0.92 × 1.43 = 1.32, so keep rolling ... 0.562 × 2 = 1.12 versus gain 0.438 × 1.05 = 0.46, so stop
key_points.reasoning: L038 gives the inequality, L041 defines Q and U, L039/L040 give both worked examples with matching values.

key_points.point_text: Tournament of 38 strategies across 2,500 head-to-head games each (3.6M total games) found FiftyPercentSurvival the champion at 69.84% win rate, and probabilistic strategies dominate the top rankings.
key_points.evidence_quote: Simulations of 38 strategies across 14 families (3.6 million games) ... FiftyPercentSurvival wins 69.84% ... the top 7 all use probability calculations
key_points.reasoning: L042 gives 38 strategies and 3.6M games; L045 gives 69.84% champion; L058 gives probabilistic dominance. The '2,500 per pairing' granularity is omitted but the structure and headline figures are intact, so full credit stands.

key_points.point_text: Consistency beats speed: GreedyUntil1Col is fastest (10.5 turns) but only ranks #11 at 58.90% due to high variance and bust rate, while FiftyPercentSurvival at 11.3 turns wins most.
key_points.evidence_quote: GreedyUntil1Col finishes in 10.5 turns but wins only 58.90%, while FiftyPercentSurvival takes 0.8 turns longer and wins 10.9% more ... The fastest strategy is not the best competitive strategy.
key_points.reasoning: L043 gives 10.5 turns with sigma 5.73 and 7.50 busts; L050/L051 give 58.90% and the consistency lesson; L064 restates that reliable 11 turns beats variable 10.5.

key_points.point_text: Significant first-player advantage: P1 wins 55.59% of games for a +11.18% edge, larger than chess (~5%) or Go (~7%); GreedyUntil1Col shows extreme bias at +31.24%.
key_points.evidence_quote: Player 1 wins 55.59%, +11.18%, larger than chess (~5%) or Go (~7%) ... GreedyUntil1Col (+31.24%)
key_points.reasoning: L065 gives 55.59%, +11.18%, and both comparison numbers; L067 gives +31.24% for GreedyUntil1Col.

key_points.point_text: Balance analysis: single-column completion times deviate at most +/-13.6% from 20 rolls, an optimal board one step from current reaches +/-3.09%, and a 20-step board reaches +/-2.17%.
key_points.evidence_quote: Single-column deviations from 20 expected rolls are at most ±13.6% ... A board one step higher per column (max 14) cuts maximum deviation to ±3.09% ... A 20-step board ... maximum deviation ±2.17%
key_points.reasoning: L074 gives ±13.6%, L080 gives ±3.09%, L081 gives ±2.17%. All three figures and their board conditions preserved.

key_points.point_text: Stated caveat: continuation versus switching strategies were not fully analyzed quantitatively and remain an open question for future work.
key_points.evidence_quote: The author has not analyzed this quantitatively; comparing 'always continue' versus 'switch when X' is left open.
key_points.reasoning: L091 explicitly preserves the open-question caveat with the same scope.

key_points.point_text: Recommendations: players should use FiftyPercentSurvival and aim for columns 5-9 while avoiding forced activation of 2-3 and 11-12; designers should prioritize playability and use rules to compensate for imbalance, considering handicaps for turn order.
key_points.evidence_quote: use FiftyPercentSurvival, aim for columns 5-9, avoid forced activation of 2-3 and 11-12, and prioritize consistency ... prioritize playability over mathematical perfection, compensate imbalances with rules, and consider turn-order handicaps
key_points.reasoning: L061 carries the player recommendation with exact column ranges and avoidance targets; L087 carries the designer recommendation including handicaps.
